title: {{NAME}} and the Fairy Who Remembered the Giants
moral: Stories keep the past alive, and the past is full of wonders.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} was digging in the riverbank when he found the tooth.

It was the size of his fist, ridged and ancient, and it glowed faintly, which teeth from the hardware store generally did not.

He dusted it off carefully. The glow pulsed once, like a heartbeat.

Then a voice no louder than the sound of a moth's wing said: "Oh. You found it."

pages.content:
The fairy's name was Thorn and she was eight hundred years old, which she mentioned several times.

"I've been looking for that for two centuries," she said, settling on {{NAME}}'s boot. "It belonged to a Triceratops. They were my friends."

{{NAME}} stared. "You knew actual dinosaurs?"

"I knew all of them. I was there at the end." She said it matter-of-factly, without drama. "Now, will you return the tooth to its owner?"

"Its owner is extinct," said {{NAME}}.

"Not entirely," said Thorn.

pages.content:
She led him deep into a forest glade where the trees were so old they had grown into each other.

At the centre, partially buried in roots and moss, was a Triceratops skull as big as a car. Its horns were intact. Its eye sockets were full of glowing moss.

Thorn flew to it and placed her hands on the bone.

{{NAME}} placed the tooth carefully back into the jaw where a socket waited for it.

The glow spread from the tooth through the whole skull, gold and slow, like sunrise.

pages.content:
The skull glowed, then settled into a warm amber hum.

Thorn told him about the Triceratops, whose name had been something like rumbling thunder: the way it had let her ride between its horns on summer evenings, the games they'd played, the storms they'd watched together from a high hill.

{{NAME}} sat cross-legged on the ground and listened to an eight-hundred-year-old fairy remember her friends, and didn't say a word, because some stories deserve that kind of quiet.

pages.content:
Thorn left before dawn, but she left him something: a tiny fossilised shell on a thread, and a note that said: ALL THE GIANTS ARE STILL HERE. YOU JUST HAVE TO KNOW WHERE TO LOOK.

{{NAME}} hung the shell above his bed and lay looking at it in the dark, thinking about all the enormous things the world used to hold.

He closed his eyes.

Somewhere in the forest, the skull glowed amber through the night, keeping eight-hundred-year-old memories warm.
